title: As Wellness Spending Grows, Can Activewear Brands Seize the Opportunity?
gist: Activewear's decade of double-digit growth is ending, decelerating to roughly 5% annually through 2030 while the broader wellness economy compounds at ~8%, so incremental growth for athletic apparel and footwear brands must come from adjacencies (nutrition/GLP-1 support, wearables, community fitness, recovery) rather than core category share. A BCG survey of 2,000+ US, German and French consumers finds wellness spending accelerates at six discrete life stages — youth sports, weight-loss journeys, new fitness goals, parenthood, injury, healthy aging — and that discovery is migrating from product search toward AI-generated recommendations, where incumbents currently hold a narrow lead.

themes.theme: Activewear growth deceleration vs. wellness-economy tailwind

insights.claim: Activewear is exiting more than a decade of double-digit expansion and is expected to grow only about 5% annually through 2030, marking a shift to a stable-growth regime.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Model activewear as a mid-single-digit grower; multiples built on double-digit category growth need to compress unless a brand is taking share or entering adjacencies.
insights.quote: activewear is entering a new era of stable growth, with the category expected to grow approximately 5% annually through 2030
insights.locator: After more than a decade of double-digit expansion

insights.claim: The global wellness economy is projected to grow roughly 8% annually, outpacing many discretionary categories and growing faster than activewear itself.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The spread between ~8% wellness growth and ~5% activewear growth is the size of the opportunity that brands must capture through adjacencies to keep growing at historical rates.
insights.quote: the global wellness economy is expected to grow approximately 8% annually, outpacing many discretionary categories
insights.locator: After more than a decade of double-digit expansion

insights.claim: Wellness registers +17% net purchase intent among surveyed consumers, ahead of technology, skincare, dining, and apparel overall, making it a defensively positioned discretionary category.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: In a consumer downturn, wellness-linked spend is a relative safe haven versus general apparel and dining exposure.
insights.quote: Wellness remains a resilient discretionary spending category with +17% net intent
insights.locator: Where Activewear Wins—and the Next Wave of Growth Beyond Apparel

insights.claim: Athletic footwear (+9%) and sportswear (+8%) show positive net spend intent over the next 12 months while broader apparel is negative at -1%, a roughly 10-point spread within the same consumer wallet.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A clear long-athletic/short-general-apparel relative signal inside consumer discretionary; watch whether the spread persists into reported comps.
insights.quote: athletic footwear (+9%) and sportswear (+8%) continuing to outperform broader apparel (–1%) on spend intent
insights.locator: Where Activewear Wins—and the Next Wave of Growth Beyond Apparel

themes.theme: Why activewear's installed base beats adjacent wellness categories

insights.claim: 94% of surveyed consumers purchase activewear, far exceeding participation in other fitness and wellness categories.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Near-universal penetration means activewear growth must come from frequency, price point, and adjacency rather than new-user acquisition.
insights.quote: 94% of consumers purchasing activewear
insights.locator: Where Activewear Wins—and the Next Wave of Growth Beyond Apparel

insights.claim: Nearly half of activewear purchasers have bought the category for over a decade, versus just 24% for connected fitness, 15% for wearables, and 13% for wellness apps — the adjacent categories are still building adoption while activewear runs on entrenched habit.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Habit tenure is the moat: activewear brands enter adjacency fights with an installed base that connected-fitness and wearables pure-plays lack.
insights.quote: Nearly half of purchasers have been buying the category for more than a decade, compared with just 24% for connected fitness, 15% for wearables, and 13% for wellness apps.

insights.claim: Physical wear-out from high-intensity use creates a recurring replacement cycle in activewear, with nearly one in three recent purchases made simply to replace worn items.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A third of demand is non-discretionary replacement, giving the category a hard revenue floor that durable-goods wellness categories do not have.
insights.quote: Nearly one in three recent purchases were simply to replace worn items.

insights.claim: Activewear's low price point relative to adjacent wellness products — connected fitness equipment can cost upwards of $1,500 — drives more frequent and impulse purchases.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Price-point asymmetry means activewear absorbs wellness enthusiasm faster than big-ticket hardware in weak consumer environments.
insights.quote: connected fitness, for example, can cost upwards of $1,500

insights.claim: Activewear's visibility in everyday life makes it a form of social signaling, particularly among younger consumers, which sustains demand beyond functional need.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Brand heat and identity marketing, not technical performance alone, drive incremental units among younger cohorts.

themes.theme: Wellness wallet share and the US-as-leading-indicator read

insights.claim: Activewear and footwear together account for only about 22% of US consumers' overall wellness spending, meaning roughly four-fifths of the wellness wallet sits outside the categories athletic brands currently sell.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Quantifies the total addressable expansion for athletic brands and sets the ceiling on what pure apparel share gains can deliver.
insights.quote: together they represent only about 22% of US consumers’ overall wellness spending
insights.locator: While activewear and footwear remain core purchases

insights.claim: In France and Germany, activewear still commands 30% to 40% of the wellness wallet versus about 22% in the US, and the US — the largest and fastest-growing wellness economy — is treated as a preview of where other markets are heading.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Implies structural wallet-share dilution ahead for European activewear as those markets mature; use US mix as the forward template for EU consumer forecasts.
insights.quote: In France and Germany, activewear still accounts for 30% to 40% of the wellness wallet.
insights.locator: While activewear and footwear remain core purchases

insights.claim: Across the US, France, and Germany, consumers indicate a growing share of future wellness spending will flow toward nutrition, weight loss solutions, gym memberships, fitness experiences, and wellness services rather than apparel.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Directs incremental wellness dollars to services and consumables operators; apparel brands must attach to those flows or watch share of wallet erode.
insights.locator: While activewear and footwear remain core purchases

themes.theme: Fitness redefined as holistic wellbeing, split by cohort

insights.claim: Building strength is the leading motivation for exercise in the survey, closely followed by improving cardiovascular health, managing weight, supporting longevity, and enhancing mental wellbeing — exercise is being reframed as overall wellbeing rather than exercise alone.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Product roadmaps and marketing anchored purely on athletic performance are misaligned with the dominant purchase motivation set.
insights.locator: Consumers are not only increasing their wellness spending

insights.claim: Older consumers emphasize cardiovascular health and healthy aging in their wellness motivations, while Gen Z and Millennials skew toward stress management and mental health.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Two distinct product and content strategies are required; a single 'performance' positioning fails both cohorts.
insights.locator: Consumers are not only increasing their wellness spending

themes.theme: Six life-stage moments as the spending-timing framework

insights.claim: Wellness spending does not expand evenly over time but accelerates at six identifiable life stages: three accelerant moments (youth sports participation, weight-loss journeys, setting a new fitness goal) and three retention moments (parenthood, injury or physical setbacks, healthy aging).
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A concrete segmentation for judging which brands' marketing and CRM spend is aimed at genuinely high-elasticity moments versus broad-brush awareness.
insights.locator: The Right Moments: When Spending Accelerates or Slows Down

insights.claim: Consumers on a weight-loss journey report activewear spend intent 31 percentage points above average, alongside higher overall wellness spending and greater participation in entirely new fitness activities.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The single largest quantified spend uplift in the study — a targetable cohort whose size scales with GLP-1 adoption.
insights.quote: consumers report activewear spend intent that is 31 percentage points above average

insights.claim: Nearly 60% of consumers say they are more willing than usual to experiment with unfamiliar activewear brands during a weight-loss journey, the clearest brand-acquisition window identified in the research.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Brand loyalty is temporarily suspended in this cohort — a share-shift window that favors challengers with targeted acquisition spend and threatens incumbents' installed base.
insights.quote: Nearly 60% of consumers report being more willing than usual to experiment with unfamiliar activewear brands during this period, making it the clearest acquisition window identified in our research.

insights.claim: During accelerant life moments the basis of competition shifts from price toward solving specific consumer goals, opening room for more specialized and higher-value offerings.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Margin expansion is available to brands that build goal-specific assortments rather than discounting into these moments.
insights.quote: the basis of competition shifts from price toward solving those needs

insights.claim: In accelerant moments consumers are not simply buying products but investing in a new version of themselves, which raises willingness to trade up and to try new brands.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Identity-driven purchase framing supports premium pricing at exactly the moments when volume is highest.
insights.quote: consumers are not simply buying products; they are investing in a new version of themselves

insights.claim: Youth sports participation creates brand preferences that can persist for years because a new sport becomes a source of social identity and consumers seek products that reinforce belonging and authenticity.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Youth sports sponsorship and team-channel investment is a long-duration customer-acquisition asset, not a marketing cost — assess brands on their presence there.

insights.claim: Setting a fitness goal such as training for a first marathon or beginning strength training is one of the strongest catalysts for increased spending on equipment, apparel, and footwear.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Goal-onset triggers are the highest-ROI targeting signal for acquisition campaigns and for AI-channel content.

insights.claim: Consumers recovering from injury show the largest decline in fitness activity and reduced activewear spending, yet many simultaneously increase spending on recovery-focused products and services.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Injury is a wallet reallocation, not a wallet contraction — brands without recovery offerings simply hand that spend to someone else.

insights.claim: Healthy aging shifts consumer spending toward preventive, low-impact, and longevity-focused solutions as fitness becomes a tool for maintaining health and independence.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Demographic aging steadily reweights the category toward walking, mobility, and low-impact product lines rather than high-performance gear.

insights.claim: Becoming a parent shifts spending away from core activewear toward wellness solutions that are convenient, adaptable, and easy to incorporate into daily routines.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Convenience-led formats (short-format fitness, at-home, subscription) capture parents that activewear brands lose by default.

themes.theme: Adjacency plays: GLP-1, wearables, community fitness, recovery

insights.claim: Nearly half of consumers navigating weight loss expect to increase activewear spending alongside higher spending on weight loss and nutrition products such as GLP-1s, making GLP-1 adoption a consumer-acquisition channel for athletic brands rather than a demand threat.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Counters the bearish 'GLP-1s shrink consumption' read for apparel — the cohort buys more activewear, not less, and is unusually brand-promiscuous.

insights.claim: GLP-1-driven body-composition change forces operational adaptation in apparel: more frequent size transitions, different replenishment cycles, and potentially higher return rates.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Watch return rates and size-curve inventory management as a margin risk and an operational differentiator among apparel retailers.

insights.claim: Wearable ownership already exceeds 65% among consumers who participate in fitness and wellness categories, and is particularly high among younger consumers.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Wearables are already mainstream inside the target consumer base, so partnership or acquisition economics are about data access, not device penetration upside.
insights.quote: wearable ownership already exceeds 65%

insights.claim: Wearable owners are more likely to exercise for athletic performance, manage body composition, and seek on-trend activewear, making them among the category's most valuable consumers.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Wearable ownership is a practical high-value-customer proxy for targeting and for valuing customer files in fitness-tech M&A.

insights.claim: Participation in the wearables space can generate consumer data that becomes an insight engine informing personalized marketing, acquisition, product development, and merchandising for apparel brands.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Frames apparel-brand interest in connected fitness as a data play, which supports a strategic-premium case for wearables and fitness-app assets.
insights.quote: plays in the wearables space have the potential to generate data that can become a valuable insight engine

insights.claim: Participants in youth sports and group fitness show above-average intent to spend both on community fitness experiences — workout classes, running clubs, fitness competitions — and on activewear, because they place high value on identity, belonging, and social signaling.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Run clubs and event ecosystems are a dual-monetization surface and an early-warning system for trend discovery; brands absent from them lose younger-cohort formation.

insights.claim: Only 4 of the top 15 apparel brands and 2 of the top 15 footwear brands currently offer dedicated recovery-focused products, leaving recovery structurally underserved even as recovery-focused fitness classes rank among the fastest-growing fitness categories globally.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A quantified whitespace: first movers into compression, temperature-regulating apparel, and walking footwear face little incumbent competition.
insights.quote: only 4 of the top 15 apparel brands and 2 of the top 15 footwear brands currently offer dedicated recovery-focused products, suggesting the category remains underserved

themes.theme: Discovery migrating from product search to AI recommendation

insights.claim: More than 60% of consumers research across four or more channels — stores, search engines, brand websites, online reviews, social media, and AI tools — before choosing an activewear brand, although stores remain the most influential touchpoint at final purchase.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Attribution models that credit the store are mismeasuring where brand choice is actually formed; multi-channel presence is table stakes.
insights.quote: more than 60% of consumers discover and research products across four or more channels before choosing an activewear brand
insights.locator: The Right Places: Winning the Next Discovery Journey

insights.claim: Established activewear brands are more likely to be discovered in stores while challenger brands rely on word of mouth, social media, and their own websites and apps; challengers lead incumbents by 2 percentage points in social and influencer discovery, while incumbents lead by 2 points in AI-driven discovery.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Contrary to the digital-native narrative, incumbents currently have the edge in AI discovery — a slim lead worth tracking as the channel scales.
insights.quote: incumbents lead by a similar margin in AI-driven discovery (+2 percentage points compared to challengers)
insights.locator: Looking more closely at how consumers discover brands

insights.claim: More than half of consumers say they are unsure which wellness products are right for them, indicating that choice proliferation has produced decision fatigue and a demand for trusted guidance rather than more information.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Decision fatigue is the demand-side driver behind AI-mediated shopping; whoever supplies the trusted recommendation captures the margin.
insights.quote: more than half saying they are unsure which wellness products are right for them
insights.locator: The intense battle for consumer attention

insights.claim: Consumer queries are shifting from single-product searches such as 'I need a new pair of running shoes' to holistic occasion questions such as 'What gear do I need to train for my first marathon?', a format AI answers better than product search because it bundles products, advice, and training plans in one experience.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Occasion-level queries disintermediate keyword SEO and retail search; the unit of competition becomes appearing inside a bundled AI answer.
insights.locator: Given this complexity, consumers are fundamentally changing

insights.claim: 36% of US consumers have used AI for shopping, 80% of those used it for product discovery, and more than 50% already use AI across wellness occasions, particularly at pivotal life stages.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Hard adoption baselines for AI commerce in a mainstream consumer category — a benchmark to track quarter over quarter against retail-media revenue.
insights.quote: Among US consumers, 36% have used AI for shopping. Of those, 80% have used it for product discovery.
insights.locator: AI is increasingly influential in driving discovery

insights.claim: Nearly one in five consumers report discovering new brands through social media or AI, rising to 29% among Gen Z.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The Gen Z gap forecasts where aggregate discovery mix lands as the cohort ages into peak spending — structurally bearish for store-led discovery moats.
insights.quote: Nearly one in five consumers report discovering new brands through social media or AI, rising to 29% among Gen Z
insights.locator: AI is increasingly influential in driving discovery

insights.claim: The same life stages that raise activewear spending and openness to new brands — starting a weight-loss journey, training for a first marathon — are the moments consumers are most likely to turn to AI for guidance, concentrating brand-switching risk in AI-mediated channels.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Highest-value acquisition moments and the least-controlled channel now coincide — brand equity built offline may not transfer into AI answers.
insights.quote: brands will need to compete for visibility within AI-generated recommendations during these high-intent consumer moments
insights.locator: For activewear brands, this creates an important new opportunity

insights.claim: Companies that establish authority in AI-generated recommendations early are expected to enjoy meaningful and durable advantages as AI becomes a more important discovery platform.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Implies a first-mover land-grab in AI visibility spend; watch which consumer brands disclose AI-channel strategies before it is priced in.
insights.quote: Companies that establish authority early will enjoy meaningful advantages as AI becomes an increasingly important discovery platform.
insights.locator: For activewear brands, this creates an important new opportunity
